I saw a whale breaching repeatedly. The whale looked really small, perhaps about 6 m long. The action was in the distance so I started taking photos with a 32 times zoom and saw some fins poking out of the water then something else. The something else is likely to be the willie of a bull whale. So I guess that a calf was putting on a display of force to try and chase the bull away from mum. Mum was swimming on her back to indicate she was not ready but the bull was swimming upside down ready to jump in when she rolled over to breath.

Field Notes - From what my dad and I could see there were three whales, probably two adults and a calf. A man who was also taking photographs said there were definietly three whales (he had a massive lense on his camera so he would have been able to see better than I could). I checked www.sawhalecentre.com and their whale sighting log stated that the whales were Southern Right Whales. These whales were sighted at about 2:10pm. We stayed there for about half an hour and then left (even though I would have enjoyed to watch them for a little longer). The whales didn't really do a lot. They raised their flippers out of the water quite a few times (it looked a bit as if they were waving at us, even though their flippers were still and not moving). I saw the whales blowing water from their (two) blowholes as well. That was it, really but it was still special to see such beautiful, curious creatures in the wild. I would love to see them again.

I think this is a big male (going on my somewhat hazy recollection of what the expert guide said),and he hung around surprisingly close to the surf break, quite content with life. Apparently, he's been returning annually for so long that he totally ignores the few local boats familiar to him, including our ecotourism vessel.
One of the approximately 18 we saw on this tour.

Another individual, seen from afar and further offshore than many, but they were scattered throughout this large relatively shallow bay. None appeared at all concerned about the presence of the vessel.(A few regulars that the tour guide has seen each winter for many years actually approached the stationary boat out of friendly curiosity but on those occasions the skipper quietly reversed or turned away at the lowest possible speed, so as to maintain the minimum allowed distance between humans and whales. **This, incidentally, was possibly one of the last such tours, because next year the minimum legal distance (currently 100m for charters, and we never got that close anyway) increases to 300m. My belief is that on-water tours won't be viable, because you can often see Southern Right Whales less than 300m offshore simply by staying on the beach, esplanade or jetty. And photograph them just as easily, especially standing on solid ground without the gentle rocking of the boat.Sad in a way, because the only extant ecotourism cruise guide here has far greater local knowledge of, and intimate connection with the increasing numbers of whales returning each winter ( for birthing not feeding, in the case of the Southern Right Whale,although a few Humpbacks are now being sighted or acoustically detected). He's been running the same on-water ecotours for many years, but would probably find alternative mariner's work, having spent most of his working life at sea.
